CHAPTER 1 OF 5 · FOOT AND ANKLE BLOCKS

Anatomy: the sciatic branches and the foot

Below the knee, everything is sciatic except one strip of skin on the inner side: the saphenous nerve, from the femoral. Learn where the sciatic nerve divides and where its five endings cross the ankle, and every block on this page follows.

KEY POINTS

The sciatic nerve (L4–S3) is two nerves in one sheath: tibial (medial) and common peroneal (lateral). They usually separate near the apex of the popliteal fossa, 5–10 cm above the crease, but the level varies and some divide high in the thigh.
At the bifurcation both nerves sit in a common paraneural sheath (sometimes called Vloka’s sheath): injection inside it is the fastest popliteal block.
Five nerves reach the foot: two deep (tibial, deep peroneal) and three superficial (superficial peroneal, sural, saphenous). Four are sciatic; the saphenous is femoral.
All the muscles below the knee are sciatic: a popliteal block weakens the whole foot and ankle (foot drop); an ankle block spares the leg muscles.
Bone and joints follow the sciatic, not the skin map: the tibia, the ankle joint and the foot bones are mainly tibial and deep peroneal, with saphenous fibres to the medial ankle.
The sciatic nerve divides
Course. Leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen below piriformis, runs under gluteus maximus midway between the ischial tuberosity and the greater trochanter, then down the back of the thigh on adductor magnus, deep to the long head of biceps femoris.
The popliteal fossa is a diamond: semitendinosus and semimembranosus above and medially, biceps femoris above and laterally, the two heads of gastrocnemius below. From superficial to deep in the middle: nerves, then the popliteal vein, then the artery.
Tibial nerve (L4–S3): straight down the middle, under gastrocnemius and soleus, to behind the medial malleolus. Muscles of the calf and the sole. Skin: the sole and heel; the medial sural cutaneous nerve.
Common peroneal nerve (L4–S2): follows the medial edge of biceps femoris to the head of the fibula, winds round the fibular neck (where it is easily compressed), and divides into the deep peroneal (front of the leg, dorsiflexion, first web space) and superficial peroneal (peronei, eversion, top of the foot). In the fossa it gives the lateral sural cutaneous nerve (outer calf) and a branch that joins the sural.
Sural nerve: usually formed from a tibial branch joined by a peroneal branch; runs down the back of the calf with the small saphenous vein to behind the lateral malleolus.
Not sciatic: the saphenous nerve (femoral, L3–L4: medial leg, medial ankle, medial foot) and the posterior femoral cutaneous nerve (S1–S3: back of the thigh and popliteal fossa, sometimes the upper calf). Neither is blocked by a popliteal block.

EXAM PEARL

Two memory hooks

“Two deep, three shallow.” The two deep nerves travel with an artery (tibial with the posterior tibial, deep peroneal with the anterior tibial): find the pulse, find the nerve. The three superficial nerves are blocked with a ring of local anaesthetic under the skin; two of them travel with a vein (sural with the small saphenous, saphenous with the great saphenous).

Behind the medial malleolus, front to back: Tom, Dick And Nervous Harry: tibialis posterior, flexor digitorum longus, artery, nerve, flexor hallucis longus.

BONES AND JOINTS (THE DEEP SUPPLY)
Ankle joint: deep peroneal (front), tibial (back and medial), with contributions from the saphenous, superficial peroneal and sural nerves. Its branches leave above the malleoli, so an ankle block does not reliably cover ankle joint surgery: use a popliteal block (plus saphenous).
Foot bones: mostly tibial (plantar nerves) and deep peroneal. A forefoot osteotomy hurts in the bone, so the deep nerves matter more than the skin map suggests.
Heel: the medial calcaneal branches of the tibial nerve can leave above the malleolus: for heel surgery, block the tibial nerve higher or use a popliteal block.

Tourniquets: which block tolerates which cuff

Ask the surgeon where the cuff goes and for how long before you choose the block. The skin under the cuff matters less than the muscle ischaemia under and below it.

WHAT COVERS IT

WHY
Cuff pain is mostly ischaemia of the muscle under and below the cuff. Every muscle below the knee is supplied by the sciatic nerve, and the saphenous nerve covers the skin on the inner side, so the popliteal plus saphenous pair covers both. The skin at the back of the upper calf is partly posterior femoral cutaneous: some patients feel the pressure there.

NOTE

Cuff safety in one breath

Pneumatic cuff, padded, at the right width; inflate after exsanguination (not by Esmarch with infection, tumour or a suspected DVT); keep the time as short as possible and tell the surgeon at an hour and at two hours; expect a rise in heart rate and blood pressure from cuff pain after 30–60 minutes under general anaesthesia, and a fall in blood pressure with a rise in end-tidal CO2 and potassium on release. Avoid a cuff over a fistula, a fracture, or severe arterial disease.

Foot drop and falls

A popliteal block takes away dorsiflexion (deep peroneal), plantarflexion and push-off (tibial) and the feeling in the sole, so the patient has no ankle control and no idea where the foot is. That is a fall waiting to happen.

Before: tell the patient the foot will be numb and weak until the next day, and why that matters.
After: non-weight-bearing on that leg (or heel weight-bearing in the surgeon’s shoe or boot, if allowed) with crutches or a frame, and an escort home for day cases. Physiotherapy checks walking before discharge.
An ankle block spares the calf and the leg muscles: the patient can walk on the heel in a post-operative shoe sooner, which is one reason it suits day-case forefoot surgery.
Weakness that outlasts the block (sensation back, weakness not): think surgical or positional causes first (a tight cast or backslab, pressure on the fibular neck, compartment syndrome), examine and document, and escalate early to the pain service, the surgeon and neurology.

WARNING

The common peroneal nerve at the fibular neck

It is the most often injured nerve in the leg: lithotomy stirrups, a lateral position without padding, a tight dressing or a backslab edge. Pad and check it at the end of every case. Its injury causes foot drop that a block can hide.

Protect the numb heel
A sciatic or popliteal block takes away the warning pain from the heel for most of a day. A heel resting on a mattress or the hard edge of a backslab can break down, especially in diabetic, vascular, frail or immobile patients.
Float the heel: a pillow under the calf, not under the heel; check casts and dressings for pressure points; turn and inspect.
No hot packs or ice directly on numb skin.
Compartment syndrome after tibial fractures and crush: agree the plan with the surgeon first. Dense, long blocks that far outlast surgery are best avoided in high-risk patients; dilute local anaesthetic without adjuncts, with trained, regular observation and compartment monitoring, does not appear to delay the diagnosis. Pain out of proportion, or new pain breaking through a working block, is compartment syndrome until proved otherwise.

CHAPTER 2 OF 5 · FOOT AND ANKLE · SCIATIC NERVE

Popliteal sciatic block

The sciatic nerve blocked in the popliteal fossa, at or just above the point where it divides into the tibial and common peroneal nerves. It numbs the whole leg below the knee, the ankle and the foot, except the strip on the inner side of the leg and the medial malleolus (saphenous, from the femoral nerve). With a saphenous block it covers all below-knee surgery and a calf tourniquet. Short on time? Jump to the pearls.

USE IT FOR

Foot and ankle surgery: fractures, arthrodesis, arthroplasty, tendon work
Calf tourniquet (with a saphenous block)
Below-knee amputation (with a saphenous or femoral block)
Achilles tendon repair, calcaneal fixation, heel surgery
Analgesia for tibial and ankle fractures; catheters for major reconstruction
POSITION
Lateral, leg on a pillow (or prone; or supine with the leg raised)
PROBE
Linear, transverse on the back of the thigh at the bifurcation
NEEDLE
80–100 mm echogenic, in-plane, lateral to medial
DOSE
15 ml of 0.4% ropivacaine (60 mg), 5 ml aliquots, inside the paraneural sheath
COVERS
Below the knee except the medial leg and medial malleolus (saphenous)

Position

Lateral, block side up, with a pillow under the leg so the knee is slightly flexed and the probe has room behind the thigh. Alternatives: prone (easiest scanning), or supine with the leg raised on a padded support or held by an assistant (fine for trauma and the obese, but the probe works from underneath).

Equipment
High-frequency linear probe (curvilinear if the nerve is deeper than about 4–5 cm)
80–100 mm echogenic short-bevel needle (the lateral entry is a long, flat path)
15 ml of 0.4% ropivacaine in a 20 ml syringe, with an extension line and an assistant to inject
Monitoring, IV access, lipid emulsion and the toxicity kit within reach
Scanning: find the bifurcation

Start at the popliteal crease, probe transverse. Colour Doppler: the popliteal artery is deepest, the vein just superficial to it, and the tibial nerve superficial to both (a bright honeycomb oval). Slide cephalad keeping the tibial nerve in view: the common peroneal nerve comes in from the lateral side, along biceps femoris, and the two meet. Block at that junction, usually 5–10 cm above the crease, but it varies: find it in every patient.

Anisotropy: the nerve fades into the fat? Tilt the probe caudally so the beam meets the nerve at right angles.
Press harder to bring a deep nerve up; pull the probe towards you (rotate your wrist, not your shoulder) for comfortable ergonomics in the obese.
See-saw sign: ask the patient to point and pull up the foot; the two nerves rock against each other.
Needle approach

In-plane, lateral to medial. Enter on the lateral thigh, 2–3 cm away from the probe, under or through biceps femoris, so that the needle runs almost parallel to the probe: it shows up brightly and reaches the nerve at its depth. The paraneural sheath tents, then gives with a pop. Stop with the tip between the tibial and common peroneal nerves, inside the sheath.

Out-of-plane (needle from caudal, tip as a bright dot walked down to the nerve) also works and suits a catheter, which then threads along the nerve.

Sonoanatomy

Labels for the OSCE: popliteal artery and vein, sciatic nerve (or tibial and common peroneal), biceps femoris (lateral), semimembranosus and semitendinosus (medial), the femur (the bright line deep, or the femoral condyles near the crease), and the paraneural sheath around both nerves.

SUPERFICIAL TO DEEP

Subcutaneous fat
Popliteal fat
Target and deposition

Fluid inside the paraneural sheath: it parts the two nerves and spreads around both, up and down the nerve. That one injection is enough. Alternatives: deep then superficial to the nerve (lift it, then wrap it), or a single injection between the two branches inside the sheath. Wrong: fluid pooling on top of the sheath (slow, patchy block), or the nerve swelling (intraneural: stop).

Dose

USUAL VOLUME AND CONCENTRATION

15 ml of 0.4% ropivacaine (60 mg)

In 5 ml aliquots, inside the paraneural sheath, aspirating between and watching the fluid wrap the nerves. Add a saphenous block (5 ml of 0.5%, 25 mg) for medial cover: total 85 mg. A common teaching maximum for a single dose of ropivacaine is about 3 mg/kg (about 210 mg at 70 kg), lower in frail older patients; use lean (ideal) body weight in the light and frail, and count every other dose given that day (surgical infiltration included). Injection should feel easy: high resistance means the tip may be against or in the nerve.

Local anaesthetic toxicity: Keep the total dose within the maximum for the patient’s weight, especially with bilateral blocks or when combining blocks.

Covers: The leg below the knee, the ankle and the foot, skin and bone, except the medial leg, medial malleolus and medial foot (saphenous).

MECHANISM

The sciatic nerve carries all the sensation below the knee except the saphenous strip, and all the muscles. At the bifurcation the tibial and common peroneal nerves share a paraneural sheath; fluid inside it spreads along both nerves for several centimetres, so one injection blocks both. The lateral sural cutaneous branch (outer upper calf) leaves the common peroneal nerve in the fossa, so a block below its origin may miss it.

HOW DENSE, HOW RELIABLE

Surgical anaesthesia of the foot and ankle when it works, with motor block (foot drop). Onset is fastest with the injection inside the sheath at the bifurcation: in a randomised trial it was about a third faster than separate injections around each nerve below the split. Test in all five territories at 15–20 minutes: a patchy block usually means only one branch was blocked.

WHAT IT MISSES
Saphenous: the medial leg, the medial malleolus and the inner foot. Add a saphenous block.
The back of the knee and thigh (posterior femoral cutaneous nerve).
A thigh tourniquet.
Complications and how to avoid them
Foot drop and falls: expected for most of a day. Crutches, no unsupported weight-bearing, escort home.
Nerve injury: the common peroneal is the lower-limb nerve most often injured around surgery (positioning and pressure at the fibular neck as well as the block), so document foot dorsiflexion before and after, and pad the fibular head. Don’t inject against high pressure, into a swollen nerve, or with pain or paraesthesia; don’t chase a twitch.
Vascular puncture: the popliteal vein and artery lie just deep to the nerves. Colour Doppler, aspirate, aliquots.
Pressure injury of the numb heel; masked compartment syndrome (agree the plan with the surgeon in tibial and ankle trauma).
Local anaesthetic toxicity when combined with other blocks and surgical infiltration.
Wrong-side block: the patient is often turned lateral or prone after the check. Stop before you block: mark visible, time-out again after positioning.
Practical pearls
Start at the crease on the artery, then follow the tibial nerve up until the peroneal joins it.
Tibial is the big one, medial; common peroneal is smaller, lateral, along biceps.
Nerve gone? Tilt the probe caudally. Still gone? Ask for a see-saw (point and pull up the foot).
Enter 2–3 cm lateral to the probe: a flat needle is a visible needle.
Inside the sheath, between the nerves: one pop, one pool, both nerves.
Fluid on top of the sheath and the nerves don’t part? Advance through it.
Medial leg still sensate = saphenous, not a failed popliteal.
Ideal for a calf cuff with a saphenous block; useless for a thigh cuff.
Numb foot, weak ankle: crutches, no weight-bearing, protect the heel.
Nerve stimulator: what the twitch tells you
Tibial nerve: plantarflexion and inversion of the foot, toe flexion. Common peroneal: dorsiflexion and eversion.
Inversion (tibialis posterior, with a deep peroneal contribution from tibialis anterior) is the classic best single response before the bifurcation: it predicts the fastest, most complete block. Eversion alone suggests you are on the peroneal nerve only.
With ultrasound, use the stimulator as a safety monitor, not a target: set about 0.5 mA and expect no twitch as you approach. A twitch at very low current (below about 0.2 mA) suggests the tip is touching or inside the nerve. But no twitch does not prove you are outside it: watch the image and the injection pressure.
Before ultrasound: landmark approaches

Exam material, and the fallback when there is no probe. Both use a nerve stimulator (start about 1–1.5 mA, aim for a twitch that persists at about 0.5 mA, as in the section above).

Posterior (intertendinous), prone: outline the triangle of the fossa: biceps femoris tendon laterally, semitendinosus and semimembranosus medially, the crease below. Enter in the midline between the tendons, classically about 7 cm above the crease, aiming cephalad. Above the bifurcation one injection reaches both nerves.
Lateral, supine: leg straight, foot free so you can watch the twitch. Enter in the groove between biceps femoris and vastus lateralis on the lateral thigh, well above the knee. Advance to the femur, withdraw and redirect posteriorly towards the nerve. Useful when the patient cannot be turned.
Twitch: inversion or plantarflexion (tibial) is the one to accept; dorsiflexion or eversion alone means the common peroneal only: redirect slightly medially.
Catheters

For major foot and ankle reconstructions, a popliteal catheter gives two to three days of analgesia. Out-of-plane from caudal (or in-plane from lateral), hydrodissect inside the sheath with 5 ml, thread 3–5 cm past the tip, then inject through the catheter while scanning to see the fluid around the nerve. Fix it well; tunnel if it must last.

Programmed intermittent boluses gave the same pain relief as a continuous infusion in a trial after major foot and ankle surgery, but a denser motor block: expect a weaker foot with bolus regimens.
Run dilute solutions (for example 0.2% ropivacaine) and plan who reviews the foot, the heel and the catheter site at home or on the ward.
Consultant corner
Bifurcation level varies. In cadavers it ranges from a few centimetres to well over 10 cm above the crease, and in some people the two nerves are separate in the thigh. If you only see two nerves, follow them up; if they never join, block each inside its own sheath (two injections) or move to a subgluteal approach.
The obese leg: curvilinear probe, a longer needle, prone or supine with the leg up; press firmly to compress fat and bring the nerve up. At some levels the common peroneal nerve lies superficial to the tibial nerve rather than beside it.
Supine with the knee flexed suits fractures and external fixators: an assistant lifts the leg, or a stack of pillows under the calf and thigh leaves the fossa free. Lateral approach needle, probe from below.
Intended subparaneural, not intraneural. Inside the paraneural sheath but outside the epineurium is the goal; ultrasound shows the nerves parting rather than swelling. Opening pressure monitoring adds protection where available.
Rebound pain the first night after a dense single shot is common after ankle fracture fixation. Give regular oral analgesia before it wears off; IV dexamethasone (usually 8 mg at induction; it raises blood glucose in diabetic patients) reduces rebound and prolongs the block by several hours, about as much as perineural use; consider a catheter for big operations.
Anticoagulated patients: the popliteal fossa is superficial and compressible; with ultrasound and a careful risk–benefit decision it is often acceptable when neuraxial is not. Follow local guidance.
Posterior knee pain after knee arthroplasty: use iPACK (on the knee page) rather than a popliteal sciatic block; it spares the common peroneal nerve and the foot.
Frontier: what’s new
Liposomal bupivacaine is now licensed in the United States for a sciatic block in the popliteal fossa (and an adductor canal block), on the basis of trials showing lower pain scores over four days than plain bupivacaine. It is not available everywhere and its added value over plain local anaesthetic with adjuncts remains debated.
Percutaneous peripheral nerve stimulation: a fine lead placed near the sciatic nerve (or the femoral nerve or brachial plexus) and stimulated for up to two weeks after ambulatory orthopaedic surgery, including foot and ankle surgery, reduced pain and opioid use in a sham-controlled pilot trial, without numbness or weakness. Combined devices that deliver both local anaesthetic and stimulation are in early trials.
Dexamethasone: IV dexamethasone prolongs the block and reduces rebound pain after ankle fracture surgery; perineural use adds a little more duration but is off-label.
Naming: the 2024 ASRA–ESRA consensus standardised limb block names as the nerve plus its anatomical location: the nerve first, then where it is blocked (here, the sciatic nerve at the popliteal fossa).
Minimum volume: dose-finding studies of the subparaneural injection suggest that much smaller volumes than the classic 30–40 ml are enough for surgical anaesthesia, which leaves room in the toxicity budget for a saphenous block and surgical infiltration.
Exam corner

MMED OSCE 2022 AND 2025

Demonstrate the sonoanatomy for a popliteal sciatic nerve block on this volunteer. Describe how you would perform the block, and what it covers.

Model answer points
Position: lateral, pillow under the leg (or prone, or supine with the leg raised). Linear probe; 80–100 mm echogenic needle.
Start at the popliteal crease: popliteal artery (deepest), vein superficial to it, tibial nerve superficial to both. Colour Doppler.
Trace cephalad until the common peroneal nerve joins the tibial nerve: the bifurcation, usually 5–10 cm above the crease.
Name: biceps femoris laterally, semimembranosus and semitendinosus medially, the femur deep, the paraneural (Vloka’s) sheath around both nerves.
In-plane, lateral to medial, entering the lateral thigh away from the probe to flatten the needle. Feel the pop through the sheath.
Target: circumferential spread inside the sheath, or a single injection between the tibial and common peroneal nerves within the sheath. 15 ml of 0.4% ropivacaine in 5 ml aliquots.
Covers the whole lower leg, ankle and foot except the anteromedial leg and medial malleolus (saphenous). Below-knee procedures; ideal for a calf tourniquet with a saphenous block.
Anisotropy: tilt caudally; press harder to bring the nerve up; out-of-plane suits a catheter. Foot drop can delay mobilisation.

The image shows a popliteal block. Label the structures. After 10 ml, the fluid sits above the nerve and the two branches have not separated. What do you do? Twenty minutes later the patient can still feel the inside of the ankle. Why?

PRACTICE QUESTION

A 70-year-old is listed for an emergency ray amputation of the right first metatarsal under a popliteal block. (a) Outline the anatomy relevant to the block. (b) The block is performed on the left leg. What may have contributed? (c) How do you manage it?

Model answer points
Anatomy: popliteal fossa boundaries (semitendinosus and semimembranosus superomedially, biceps femoris superolaterally, the two heads of gastrocnemius inferiorly); contents superficial to deep: nerve, vein, artery; sciatic nerve dividing near the apex, at a variable level; common paraneural sheath.
Contributors: emergency, after hours, remote site, fatigue, distraction, no visible site mark after positioning, no repeat time-out after turning the patient, junior unsupervised operator, patient unable to verify (unwell or sedated).
Management: stop; check total dose given; open disclosure to the patient; choose the anaesthetic: repeat block on the correct side only if within the safe dose, or spinal, or general anaesthesia.
Monitor for local anaesthetic toxicity; protect the wrongly blocked leg (falls, heel); follow up for nerve injury.
Document, report as an incident, and review at the department (Stop Before You Block).

PRACTICE QUESTION

A 45-year-old has an open reduction and internal fixation of a bimalleolar ankle fracture. The surgeon is worried about compartment syndrome. Plan the anaesthetic and analgesia.

Model answer points
Discuss with the surgeon first; document the plan and the patient’s consent.
Spinal or general anaesthesia for surgery and the thigh cuff.
If blocks are used: popliteal sciatic plus saphenous with dilute local anaesthetic, no adjuncts, single shot, timed so the block does not long outlast surgery; or no block and multimodal analgesia if the risk is high.
Trained, regular ward observation; low threshold for compartment pressure measurement; breakthrough or escalating pain is a red flag, not a failed block.
Multimodal: paracetamol, an NSAID if suitable, IV dexamethasone (reduces rebound pain), opioid rescue planned before the block wears off.

Position

Supine, with a roll or a footrest under the calf so the heel and both malleoli are free and you can reach behind them. Externally rotate the leg for the tibial and saphenous nerves; internally rotate it for the sural. Stand at the foot of the bed for the front of the ankle.

Equipment
High-frequency linear probe (a small footprint helps behind the malleoli)
50 mm echogenic needle for the deep nerves; 23–25G hypodermic for rings
17 ml of 0.5% ropivacaine (more volume, same dose limit, for a landmark block)
Colour Doppler: the two deep nerves are found by their arteries
Order and scanning

Tibial first: it is the biggest nerve with the slowest onset, and it supplies the sole. Then the deep peroneal, then the three superficial nerves. The scan viewer below shows the tibial nerve; the other four are under Ultrasound, nerve by nerve; the classic landmark ring is under Landmark technique.

Tibial: behind the medial malleolus, posterior to the posterior tibial artery. Scanning a few centimetres higher catches the calcaneal branches and keeps the probe off the bone.
Deep peroneal: front of the ankle beside the anterior tibial artery on the tibia, between EHL and EDL. It may lie medial or lateral to the artery: find it on each scan.
Superficial peroneal: above the fascia over the peroneus brevis–EDL groove, about 10 cm above the lateral malleolus, before it divides.
Sural: beside the small saphenous vein between the lateral malleolus and the Achilles tendon.
Saphenous: beside the great saphenous vein in front of the medial malleolus. Light pressure for both veins.
Needle approach

In-plane at each site, short and shallow; the direction follows comfort (the scan viewers use posterior to anterior for the tibial nerve, lateral to medial for the deep peroneal). One well-placed deposit is enough: these nerves are small and take up local anaesthetic quickly, so you don’t need to redirect for full circumferential spread. Keep off the periosteum: injection under it is painful.

Sonoanatomy

Tibial: Tom, Dick, Artery, Nerve, Harry (tibialis posterior, flexor digitorum longus, posterior tibial artery, tibial nerve, flexor hallucis longus) under the flexor retinaculum. Tendon or nerve? Target and deposition

Deep nerves: fluid ringing the nerve beneath the retinaculum (flexor at the back, extensor at the front). Fluid spreading under the skin superficial to the retinaculum will not reach the nerve. Superficial nerves: fluid around the nerve, or around its vein when the nerve cannot be seen; without ultrasound, a continuous subcutaneous ring between the landmarks.

Deep peroneal (deep): between the extensor hallucis longus and extensor digitorum longus tendons, just lateral to the dorsalis pedis pulse; down to bone, back 1–2 mm, aspirate, 3–5 ml.
Superficial peroneal (ring): subcutaneously from the front of the tibia to the lateral malleolus.

Saphenous (ring): subcutaneously from the medial malleolus to the front of the ankle, around the great saphenous vein; aspirate.

The three rings can be joined into one band round the front of the ankle from malleolus to malleolus. Theoretically avoid adrenaline. Expect it to sting more and to fail more often than the ultrasound block: test each territory.

Consultant corner
Fit the block to the operation. The saphenous territory usually ends at the medial midfoot, short of the first tarsometatarsal joint, so for bunion and other forefoot surgery it can usually be left out. Include it when the incision extends back towards the midfoot, or for medial midfoot and ankle work. Ankle and hindfoot surgery need a popliteal block, because the joint branches leave higher.
Supramalleolar (“high”) ankle block: blocking all five about 10 cm above the malleoli catches the nerves before they branch (the superficial peroneal and the calcaneal branches) and keeps the probe on soft tissue. The deep peroneal is then deep between tibialis anterior and EHL on the interosseous membrane.
Diabetic and vascular feet: document pre-existing neuropathy; no adrenaline; avoid injecting through cellulitis or ulcers. The ankle block avoids general anaesthesia and spares the leg for early mobility.
Combining with general anaesthesia: a laryngeal mask plus ankle block is a common day-case recipe; the block provides the analgesia and lets the patient go home walking on the heel.
Bilateral surgery: two ultrasound ankle blocks (170 mg) fit within the maximum dose for most adults over about 60 kg, and avoid bilateral foot drop. Calculate by weight, reduce the concentration or volume in small or frail patients, and remember the surgeon’s infiltration.
Rescue: after a popliteal block, a single missed territory can be topped up at the ankle (for example the saphenous ring or the superficial peroneal).
Frontier: what’s new
Ultrasound versus landmarks: the gain is clearest for the tibial nerve; for the deep peroneal nerve, ultrasound did not beat a careful landmark technique beyond the first 20 minutes in volunteers. Spend your scanning time behind the medial malleolus.
Ankle cuffs under ankle block: a large audit showed the cuff is comfortable for most patients for about half an hour, with tolerance falling with time and in patients over 70: plan sedation or a calf cuff with a popliteal block for long cases.
Vein as the target: for the sural nerve, ringing the small saphenous vein under ultrasound gave a faster, denser and longer block than the landmark ring in volunteers. The same perivenous logic works for the saphenous nerve with the great saphenous vein.
Long-acting options: IV dexamethasone prolongs single-shot blocks; liposomal bupivacaine is licensed in some countries for other lower-limb blocks. For a day-case forefoot block, plain long-acting local anaesthetic with regular oral analgesia remains the standard.

Tibial (sciatic): sole and heel; behind the medial malleolus, posterior to the posterior tibial artery, midway to the Achilles.
Deep peroneal (common peroneal): first web space; between EHL and EDL, beside the dorsalis pedis/anterior tibial artery.
Superficial peroneal (common peroneal): most of the dorsum except the first web space; subcutaneous ring from the tibial crest to the lateral malleolus.

Saphenous (femoral): medial ankle and foot; subcutaneous in front of the medial malleolus, around the great saphenous vein.

Where to block it

The nerve leaves the adductor canal in the distal thigh, runs down between sartorius and gracilis to the medial knee, gives off the infrapatellar branch (skin below and inside the kneecap), then pierces the fascia and runs down the medial leg with the great saphenous vein to the front of the medial malleolus.

Distal thigh, at the end of the adductor canal (distal subsartorial, or transsartorial): more reliable for the foot, still quadriceps-sparing when done low enough. See At the knee and above.
Adductor canal or femoral triangle: on the knee page; reliable but higher blocks can weaken vastus medialis.
Needle approach

Ultrasound: in-plane, shallow, in the fat; either direction. The tip stops next to the vein, on the nerve’s side, not in the vein. Keep probe pressure light or the vein (your landmark) disappears.

With a popliteal block (60 mg) the total is 85–110 mg: count it, and any surgical infiltration, against the patient’s maximum (about 3 mg/kg of ropivacaine, 210 mg at 70 kg). 0.5% matches the long popliteal block it usually accompanies; for the saphenous nerve on its own, 0.375% works as well.

Even without ultrasound, injecting beside the visible vein blocked the nerve in all 20 volunteers in its first description, against about a third with blind subcutaneous infiltration; with ultrasound the success is high (around 90% in a trial of the infracondylar approach). The knee (infrapatellar branch, femoral and obturator branches).
Everything else below the knee: it is a companion to a popliteal or ankle block, not a block on its own for most surgery.

Find the vein, find the nerve. Light pressure, or the vein vanishes.
A thigh band fills the vein and makes the target obvious.

Below-knee blocks spare the knee skin and the quadriceps.

Which saphenous block for which job. Forefoot: often not needed. Medial ankle, ankle fixation, medial malleolus: a distal adductor canal or below-knee paravenous block. Varicose veins, obesity, oedema make the paravenous view harder; go up to the distal adductor canal, where the artery is the landmark.

Distal subsartorial compartment block: a recently described target just distal to the adductor hiatus, aimed at blocking the saphenous nerve alone for foot and ankle surgery while sparing the quadriceps.
Distal adductor canal or below the knee? For foot and ankle surgery both spare the quadriceps when the injection is distal to the nerve to vastus medialis. The distal canal block uses the artery as its landmark and covers the medial foot more reliably; the below-knee paravenous block avoids the thigh altogether but depends on finding the vein. Choose by body habitus, the veins, and whether the patient is lateral or supine for the popliteal block.
Selective infrapatellar branch blocks are being mapped with ultrasound for knee arthroscopy and to treat painful infrapatellar neuromas after knee surgery.
Exam corner

A patient has had a popliteal sciatic block for an ankle fracture fixation. The medial malleolus and the medial side of the incision are still sensate. Explain why, and describe two ways to block the nerve responsible.

Model answer points
The saphenous nerve (terminal sensory branch of the femoral nerve, L3–L4) supplies the medial leg, the medial malleolus and the inner foot; it is not part of the sciatic nerve.
Ultrasound paravenous block below the knee: transverse at the tibial tuberosity, thigh band to fill the great saphenous vein, in-plane, 5 ml around the vein.
Distal adductor canal (subsartorial) block: 5–10 ml under sartorius near the adductor hiatus; reliable for the foot, quadriceps largely spared.
Landmark field block: 5–10 ml subcutaneously from the tibial tuberosity to medial gastrocnemius, injecting while withdrawing; less reliable.
Check the total local anaesthetic dose with the popliteal block.

PRACTICE QUESTION

Compare the approaches to the saphenous nerve for foot and ankle surgery.

Model answer points
Femoral triangle / mid-thigh adductor canal: reliable, may weaken vastus medialis and the quadriceps.
Distal adductor canal / subsartorial / transsartorial: reliable for the foot, quadriceps spared when done low.
Below the knee, paravenous with ultrasound: simple, superficial, high success; harder with varicose veins or obesity; vein puncture.
Below-knee landmark field block: no equipment, but the least reliable and more painful.
At the ankle: in front of the medial malleolus around the great saphenous vein; covers only the medial ankle and foot.

CHAPTER 1 OF 5 · FOOT AND ANKLE BLOCKS

Anatomy: the sciatic branches and the foot

Below the knee, everything is sciatic except one strip of skin on the inner side: the saphenous nerve, from the femoral. Learn where the sciatic nerve divides and where its five endings cross the ankle, and every block on this page follows.

KEY POINTS

The sciatic nerve (L4–S3) is two nerves in one sheath: tibial (medial) and common peroneal (lateral). They usually separate near the apex of the popliteal fossa, 5–10 cm above the crease, but the level varies and some divide high in the thigh.
At the bifurcation both nerves sit in a common paraneural sheath (sometimes called Vloka’s sheath): injection inside it is the fastest popliteal block.
Five nerves reach the foot: two deep (tibial, deep peroneal) and three superficial (superficial peroneal, sural, saphenous). Four are sciatic; the saphenous is femoral.
All the muscles below the knee are sciatic: a popliteal block weakens the whole foot and ankle (foot drop); an ankle block spares the leg muscles.
Bone and joints follow the sciatic, not the skin map: the tibia, the ankle joint and the foot bones are mainly tibial and deep peroneal, with saphenous fibres to the medial ankle.
The sciatic nerve divides
Course. Leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen below piriformis, runs under gluteus maximus midway between the ischial tuberosity and the greater trochanter, then down the back of the thigh on adductor magnus, deep to the long head of biceps femoris.
The popliteal fossa is a diamond: semitendinosus and semimembranosus above and medially, biceps femoris above and laterally, the two heads of gastrocnemius below. From superficial to deep in the middle: nerves, then the popliteal vein, then the artery.
Tibial nerve (L4–S3): straight down the middle, under gastrocnemius and soleus, to behind the medial malleolus. Muscles of the calf and the sole. Skin: the sole and heel; the medial sural cutaneous nerve.
Common peroneal nerve (L4–S2): follows the medial edge of biceps femoris to the head of the fibula, winds round the fibular neck (where it is easily compressed), and divides into the deep peroneal (front of the leg, dorsiflexion, first web space) and superficial peroneal (peronei, eversion, top of the foot). In the fossa it gives the lateral sural cutaneous nerve (outer calf) and a branch that joins the sural.
Sural nerve: usually formed from a tibial branch joined by a peroneal branch; runs down the back of the calf with the small saphenous vein to behind the lateral malleolus.
Not sciatic: the saphenous nerve (femoral, L3–L4: medial leg, medial ankle, medial foot) and the posterior femoral cutaneous nerve (S1–S3: back of the thigh and popliteal fossa, sometimes the upper calf). Neither is blocked by a popliteal block.

WHAT COVERS IT
Popliteal sciatic + saphenous. An ankle block alone is not enough.
WHY
Cuff pain is mostly ischaemia of the muscle under and below the cuff. Every muscle below the knee is supplied by the sciatic nerve, and the saphenous nerve covers the skin on the inner side, so the popliteal plus saphenous pair covers both. The skin at the back of the upper calf is partly posterior femoral cutaneous: some patients feel the pressure there.

NOTE

Cuff safety in one breath

Pneumatic cuff, padded, at the right width; inflate after exsanguination (not by Esmarch with infection, tumour or a suspected DVT); keep the time as short as possible and tell the surgeon at an hour and at two hours; expect a rise in heart rate and blood pressure from cuff pain after 30–60 minutes under general anaesthesia, and a fall in blood pressure with a rise in end-tidal CO2 and potassium on release. Avoid a cuff over a fistula, a fracture, or severe arterial disease.

Foot drop and falls

A popliteal block takes away dorsiflexion (deep peroneal), plantarflexion and push-off (tibial) and the feeling in the sole, so the patient has no ankle control and no idea where the foot is. That is a fall waiting to happen.

Before: tell the patient the foot will be numb and weak until the next day, and why that matters.
After: non-weight-bearing on that leg (or heel weight-bearing in the surgeon’s shoe or boot, if allowed) with crutches or a frame, and an escort home for day cases. Physiotherapy checks walking before discharge.
An ankle block spares the calf and the leg muscles: the patient can walk on the heel in a post-operative shoe sooner, which is one reason it suits day-case forefoot surgery.
Weakness that outlasts the block (sensation back, weakness not): think surgical or positional causes first (a tight cast or backslab, pressure on the fibular neck, compartment syndrome), examine and document, and escalate early to the pain service, the surgeon and neurology.

WARNING

The common peroneal nerve at the fibular neck

It is the most often injured nerve in the leg: lithotomy stirrups, a lateral position without padding, a tight dressing or a backslab edge. Pad and check it at the end of every case. Its injury causes foot drop that a block can hide.

Protect the numb heel
A sciatic or popliteal block takes away the warning pain from the heel for most of a day. A heel resting on a mattress or the hard edge of a backslab can break down, especially in diabetic, vascular, frail or immobile patients.
Float the heel: a pillow under the calf, not under the heel; check casts and dressings for pressure points; turn and inspect.
No hot packs or ice directly on numb skin.
Compartment syndrome after tibial fractures and crush: agree the plan with the surgeon first. Dense, long blocks that far outlast surgery are best avoided in high-risk patients; dilute local anaesthetic without adjuncts, with trained, regular observation and compartment monitoring, does not appear to delay the diagnosis. Pain out of proportion, or new pain breaking through a working block, is compartment syndrome until proved otherwise.

Popliteal sciatic block

The sciatic nerve blocked in the popliteal fossa, at or just above the point where it divides into the tibial and common peroneal nerves. Position

Lateral, block side up, with a pillow under the leg so the knee is slightly flexed and the probe has room behind the thigh. Alternatives: prone (easiest scanning), or supine with the leg raised on a padded support or held by an assistant (fine for trauma and the obese, but the probe works from underneath).

Equipment
High-frequency linear probe (curvilinear if the nerve is deeper than about 4–5 cm)
80–100 mm echogenic short-bevel needle (the lateral entry is a long, flat path)
15 ml of 0.4% ropivacaine in a 20 ml syringe, with an extension line and an assistant to inject
Monitoring, IV access, lipid emulsion and the toxicity kit within reach
Scanning: find the bifurcation

Start at the popliteal crease, probe transverse. Colour Doppler: the popliteal artery is deepest, the vein just superficial to it, and the tibial nerve superficial to both (a bright honeycomb oval). Slide cephalad keeping the tibial nerve in view: the common peroneal nerve comes in from the lateral side, along biceps femoris, and the two meet. Block at that junction, usually 5–10 cm above the crease, but it varies: find it in every patient.

Anisotropy: the nerve fades into the fat? Tilt the probe caudally so the beam meets the nerve at right angles.
Press harder to bring a deep nerve up; pull the probe towards you (rotate your wrist, not your shoulder) for comfortable ergonomics in the obese.
See-saw sign: ask the patient to point and pull up the foot; the two nerves rock against each other.
Needle approach

In-plane, lateral to medial. Enter on the lateral thigh, 2–3 cm away from the probe, under or through biceps femoris, so that the needle runs almost parallel to the probe: it shows up brightly and reaches the nerve at its depth. The paraneural sheath tents, then gives with a pop. Stop with the tip between the tibial and common peroneal nerves, inside the sheath.

Out-of-plane (needle from caudal, tip as a bright dot walked down to the nerve) also works and suits a catheter, which then threads along the nerve.

Sonoanatomy

Labels for the OSCE: popliteal artery and vein, sciatic nerve (or tibial and common peroneal), biceps femoris (lateral), semimembranosus and semitendinosus (medial), the femur (the bright line deep, or the femoral condyles near the crease), and the paraneural sheath around both nerves.

SUPERFICIAL TO DEEP

Subcutaneous fat
Popliteal fat
Target and deposition

Fluid inside the paraneural sheath: it parts the two nerves and spreads around both, up and down the nerve. That one injection is enough. Alternatives: deep then superficial to the nerve (lift it, then wrap it), or a single injection between the two branches inside the sheath. Wrong: fluid pooling on top of the sheath (slow, patchy block), or the nerve swelling (intraneural: stop).

Dose

USUAL VOLUME AND CONCENTRATION

15 ml of 0.4% ropivacaine (60 mg)

In 5 ml aliquots, inside the paraneural sheath, aspirating between and watching the fluid wrap the nerves. Add a saphenous block (5 ml of 0.5%, 25 mg) for medial cover: total 85 mg. A common teaching maximum for a single dose of ropivacaine is about 3 mg/kg (about 210 mg at 70 kg), lower in frail older patients; use lean (ideal) body weight in the light and frail, and count every other dose given that day (surgical infiltration included). Injection should feel easy: high resistance means the tip may be against or in the nerve.

Local anaesthetic toxicity: Keep the total dose within the maximum for the patient’s weight, especially with bilateral blocks or when combining blocks.

Covers: The leg below the knee, the ankle and the foot, skin and bone, except the medial leg, medial malleolus and medial foot (saphenous).

MECHANISM

The sciatic nerve carries all the sensation below the knee except the saphenous strip, and all the muscles. At the bifurcation the tibial and common peroneal nerves share a paraneural sheath; fluid inside it spreads along both nerves for several centimetres, so one injection blocks both. The lateral sural cutaneous branch (outer upper calf) leaves the common peroneal nerve in the fossa, so a block below its origin may miss it.

HOW DENSE, HOW RELIABLE

Surgical anaesthesia of the foot and ankle when it works, with motor block (foot drop). Onset is fastest with the injection inside the sheath at the bifurcation: in a randomised trial it was about a third faster than separate injections around each nerve below the split. Test in all five territories at 15–20 minutes: a patchy block usually means only one branch was blocked.

WHAT IT MISSES
Saphenous: the medial leg, the medial malleolus and the inner foot. Add a saphenous block.
The back of the knee and thigh (posterior femoral cutaneous nerve).
A thigh tourniquet.
Complications and how to avoid them
Foot drop and falls: expected for most of a day. Crutches, no unsupported weight-bearing, escort home.
Nerve injury: the common peroneal is the lower-limb nerve most often injured around surgery (positioning and pressure at the fibular neck as well as the block), so document foot dorsiflexion before and after, and pad the fibular head. Don’t inject against high pressure, into a swollen nerve, or with pain or paraesthesia; don’t chase a twitch.
Vascular puncture: the popliteal vein and artery lie just deep to the nerves. Colour Doppler, aspirate, aliquots.
Pressure injury of the numb heel; masked compartment syndrome (agree the plan with the surgeon in tibial and ankle trauma).
Local anaesthetic toxicity when combined with other blocks and surgical infiltration.
Wrong-side block: the patient is often turned lateral or prone after the check. Stop before you block: mark visible, time-out again after positioning.
Practical pearls
Start at the crease on the artery, then follow the tibial nerve up until the peroneal joins it.
Tibial is the big one, medial; common peroneal is smaller, lateral, along biceps.
Nerve gone? Tilt the probe caudally. Still gone? Ask for a see-saw (point and pull up the foot).
Enter 2–3 cm lateral to the probe: a flat needle is a visible needle.
Inside the sheath, between the nerves: one pop, one pool, both nerves.
Fluid on top of the sheath and the nerves don’t part? Advance through it.
Medial leg still sensate = saphenous, not a failed popliteal.
Ideal for a calf cuff with a saphenous block; useless for a thigh cuff.
Numb foot, weak ankle: crutches, no weight-bearing, protect the heel.
Nerve stimulator: what the twitch tells you
Tibial nerve: plantarflexion and inversion of the foot, toe flexion. Common peroneal: dorsiflexion and eversion.
Inversion (tibialis posterior, with a deep peroneal contribution from tibialis anterior) is the classic best single response before the bifurcation: it predicts the fastest, most complete block. Eversion alone suggests you are on the peroneal nerve only.
With ultrasound, use the stimulator as a safety monitor, not a target: set about 0.5 mA and expect no twitch as you approach. A twitch at very low current (below about 0.2 mA) suggests the tip is touching or inside the nerve. But no twitch does not prove you are outside it: watch the image and the injection pressure.
Before ultrasound: landmark approaches

Exam material, and the fallback when there is no probe. Both use a nerve stimulator (start about 1–1.5 mA, aim for a twitch that persists at about 0.5 mA, as in the section above).

Posterior (intertendinous), prone: outline the triangle of the fossa: biceps femoris tendon laterally, semitendinosus and semimembranosus medially, the crease below. Enter in the midline between the tendons, classically about 7 cm above the crease, aiming cephalad. Above the bifurcation one injection reaches both nerves.
Lateral, supine: leg straight, foot free so you can watch the twitch. Enter in the groove between biceps femoris and vastus lateralis on the lateral thigh, well above the knee. Advance to the femur, withdraw and redirect posteriorly towards the nerve. Useful when the patient cannot be turned.
Twitch: inversion or plantarflexion (tibial) is the one to accept; dorsiflexion or eversion alone means the common peroneal only: redirect slightly medially.
Catheters

For major foot and ankle reconstructions, a popliteal catheter gives two to three days of analgesia. Out-of-plane from caudal (or in-plane from lateral), hydrodissect inside the sheath with 5 ml, thread 3–5 cm past the tip, then inject through the catheter while scanning to see the fluid around the nerve. Fix it well; tunnel if it must last.

Programmed intermittent boluses gave the same pain relief as a continuous infusion in a trial after major foot and ankle surgery, but a denser motor block: expect a weaker foot with bolus regimens.
Run dilute solutions (for example 0.2% ropivacaine) and plan who reviews the foot, the heel and the catheter site at home or on the ward.
Consultant corner
Bifurcation level varies. In cadavers it ranges from a few centimetres to well over 10 cm above the crease, and in some people the two nerves are separate in the thigh. If you only see two nerves, follow them up; if they never join, block each inside its own sheath (two injections) or move to a subgluteal approach.
The obese leg: curvilinear probe, a longer needle, prone or supine with the leg up; press firmly to compress fat and bring the nerve up. At some levels the common peroneal nerve lies superficial to the tibial nerve rather than beside it.
Supine with the knee flexed suits fractures and external fixators: an assistant lifts the leg, or a stack of pillows under the calf and thigh leaves the fossa free. Lateral approach needle, probe from below.
Intended subparaneural, not intraneural. Inside the paraneural sheath but outside the epineurium is the goal; ultrasound shows the nerves parting rather than swelling. Opening pressure monitoring adds protection where available.
Rebound pain the first night after a dense single shot is common after ankle fracture fixation. Give regular oral analgesia before it wears off; IV dexamethasone (usually 8 mg at induction; it raises blood glucose in diabetic patients) reduces rebound and prolongs the block by several hours, about as much as perineural use; consider a catheter for big operations.
Anticoagulated patients: the popliteal fossa is superficial and compressible; with ultrasound and a careful risk–benefit decision it is often acceptable when neuraxial is not. Follow local guidance.
Posterior knee pain after knee arthroplasty: use iPACK (on the knee page) rather than a popliteal sciatic block; it spares the common peroneal nerve and the foot.
Frontier: what’s new
Liposomal bupivacaine is now licensed in the United States for a sciatic block in the popliteal fossa (and an adductor canal block), on the basis of trials showing lower pain scores over four days than plain bupivacaine. It is not available everywhere and its added value over plain local anaesthetic with adjuncts remains debated.
Percutaneous peripheral nerve stimulation: a fine lead placed near the sciatic nerve (or the femoral nerve or brachial plexus) and stimulated for up to two weeks after ambulatory orthopaedic surgery, including foot and ankle surgery, reduced pain and opioid use in a sham-controlled pilot trial, without numbness or weakness. Combined devices that deliver both local anaesthetic and stimulation are in early trials.
Dexamethasone: IV dexamethasone prolongs the block and reduces rebound pain after ankle fracture surgery; perineural use adds a little more duration but is off-label.
Naming: the 2024 ASRA–ESRA consensus standardised limb block names as the nerve plus its anatomical location: the nerve first, then where it is blocked (here, the sciatic nerve at the popliteal fossa).
Minimum volume: dose-finding studies of the subparaneural injection suggest that much smaller volumes than the classic 30–40 ml are enough for surgical anaesthesia, which leaves room in the toxicity budget for a saphenous block and surgical infiltration.
Exam corner

MMED OSCE 2022 AND 2025

Model answer points
Position: lateral, pillow under the leg (or prone, or supine with the leg raised). Linear probe; 80–100 mm echogenic needle.
Start at the popliteal crease: popliteal artery (deepest), vein superficial to it, tibial nerve superficial to both. Colour Doppler.
Trace cephalad until the common peroneal nerve joins the tibial nerve: the bifurcation, usually 5–10 cm above the crease.
Name: biceps femoris laterally, semimembranosus and semitendinosus medially, the femur deep, the paraneural (Vloka’s) sheath around both nerves.
In-plane, lateral to medial, entering the lateral thigh away from the probe to flatten the needle. Feel the pop through the sheath.
Target: circumferential spread inside the sheath, or a single injection between the tibial and common peroneal nerves within the sheath. 15 ml of 0.4% ropivacaine in 5 ml aliquots.

PRACTICE QUESTION

The image shows a popliteal block. Label the structures. After 10 ml, the fluid sits above the nerve and the two branches have not separated. What do you do? Twenty minutes later the patient can still feel the inside of the ankle. Why?

Keep within the dose limit: count what has already been given.

A 70-year-old is listed for an emergency ray amputation of the right first metatarsal under a popliteal block. (a) Outline the anatomy relevant to the block. (b) The block is performed on the left leg. What may have contributed? (c) How do you manage it?

Model answer points
Anatomy: popliteal fossa boundaries (semitendinosus and semimembranosus superomedially, biceps femoris superolaterally, the two heads of gastrocnemius inferiorly); contents superficial to deep: nerve, vein, artery; sciatic nerve dividing near the apex, at a variable level; common paraneural sheath.
Contributors: emergency, after hours, remote site, fatigue, distraction, no visible site mark after positioning, no repeat time-out after turning the patient, junior unsupervised operator, patient unable to verify (unwell or sedated).
Management: stop; check total dose given; open disclosure to the patient; choose the anaesthetic: repeat block on the correct side only if within the safe dose, or spinal, or general anaesthesia.
Monitor for local anaesthetic toxicity; protect the wrongly blocked leg (falls, heel); follow up for nerve injury.
Document, report as an incident, and review at the department (Stop Before You Block).

PRACTICE QUESTION

A 45-year-old has an open reduction and internal fixation of a bimalleolar ankle fracture. The surgeon is worried about compartment syndrome. Plan the anaesthetic and analgesia.

Model answer points
Discuss with the surgeon first; document the plan and the patient’s consent.
Spinal or general anaesthesia for surgery and the thigh cuff.
If blocks are used: popliteal sciatic plus saphenous with dilute local anaesthetic, no adjuncts, single shot, timed so the block does not long outlast surgery; or no block and multimodal analgesia if the risk is high.
Trained, regular ward observation; low threshold for compartment pressure measurement; breakthrough or escalating pain is a red flag, not a failed block.
Multimodal: paracetamol, an NSAID if suitable, IV dexamethasone (reduces rebound pain), opioid rescue planned before the block wears off.

Ankle block

Position

Supine, with a roll or a footrest under the calf so the heel and both malleoli are free and you can reach behind them. Externally rotate the leg for the tibial and saphenous nerves; internally rotate it for the sural. Stand at the foot of the bed for the front of the ankle.

Order and scanning

Tibial first: it is the biggest nerve with the slowest onset, and it supplies the sole. Then the deep peroneal, then the three superficial nerves. The scan viewer below shows the tibial nerve; the other four are under Ultrasound, nerve by nerve; the classic landmark ring is under Landmark technique.

Tibial: behind the medial malleolus, posterior to the posterior tibial artery. Scanning a few centimetres higher catches the calcaneal branches and keeps the probe off the bone.
Deep peroneal: front of the ankle beside the anterior tibial artery on the tibia, between EHL and EDL. It may lie medial or lateral to the artery: find it on each scan.
Superficial peroneal: above the fascia over the peroneus brevis–EDL groove, about 10 cm above the lateral malleolus, before it divides.
Sural: beside the small saphenous vein between the lateral malleolus and the Achilles tendon.
Saphenous: beside the great saphenous vein in front of the medial malleolus. Light pressure for both veins.
Needle approach

In-plane at each site, short and shallow; the direction follows comfort (the scan viewers use posterior to anterior for the tibial nerve, lateral to medial for the deep peroneal). One well-placed deposit is enough: these nerves are small and take up local anaesthetic quickly, so you don’t need to redirect for full circumferential spread. Keep off the periosteum: injection under it is painful.

Vascular puncture and bruising: posterior tibial and dorsalis pedis arteries; the saphenous vein is the one most often hit. Aspirate.
Nerve injury: rare; don’t inject against resistance or with sharp pain.
Toxicity: low risk at these doses, but count when bilateral or combined.
Ischaemia: no adrenaline in a digital ring, and avoid it at the ankle when the circulation is poor.

Two deep (with an artery), three shallow (two with a vein).
Tibial first: biggest nerve, slowest onset, the whole sole.
Scan the tibial nerve a hand’s breadth up: off the bone, before the heel branches.
Tendon or nerve? Slide up. Tendons become muscle; nerves stay nerves.
Deep peroneal can be on either side of the artery: find it, don’t assume.

Ankle cuff yes; calf cuff no.

Consultant corner
Fit the block to the operation. The saphenous territory usually ends at the medial midfoot, short of the first tarsometatarsal joint, so for bunion and other forefoot surgery it can usually be left out. Include it when the incision extends back towards the midfoot, or for medial midfoot and ankle work. Ankle and hindfoot surgery need a popliteal block, because the joint branches leave higher.
Supramalleolar (“high”) ankle block: blocking all five about 10 cm above the malleoli catches the nerves before they branch (the superficial peroneal and the calcaneal branches) and keeps the probe on soft tissue. The deep peroneal is then deep between tibialis anterior and EHL on the interosseous membrane.
Diabetic and vascular feet: document pre-existing neuropathy; no adrenaline; avoid injecting through cellulitis or ulcers. The ankle block avoids general anaesthesia and spares the leg for early mobility.
Combining with general anaesthesia: a laryngeal mask plus ankle block is a common day-case recipe; the block provides the analgesia and lets the patient go home walking on the heel.
Bilateral surgery: two ultrasound ankle blocks (170 mg) fit within the maximum dose for most adults over about 60 kg, and avoid bilateral foot drop. Calculate by weight, reduce the concentration or volume in small or frail patients, and remember the surgeon’s infiltration.
Rescue: after a popliteal block, a single missed territory can be topped up at the ankle (for example the saphenous ring or the superficial peroneal).
Frontier: what’s new
Ultrasound versus landmarks: the gain is clearest for the tibial nerve; for the deep peroneal nerve, ultrasound did not beat a careful landmark technique beyond the first 20 minutes in volunteers. Spend your scanning time behind the medial malleolus.
Ankle cuffs under ankle block: a large audit showed the cuff is comfortable for most patients for about half an hour, with tolerance falling with time and in patients over 70: plan sedation or a calf cuff with a popliteal block for long cases.
Vein as the target: for the sural nerve, ringing the small saphenous vein under ultrasound gave a faster, denser and longer block than the landmark ring in volunteers. The same perivenous logic works for the saphenous nerve with the great saphenous vein.
Long-acting options: IV dexamethasone prolongs single-shot blocks; liposomal bupivacaine is licensed in some countries for other lower-limb blocks. For a day-case forefoot block, plain long-acting local anaesthetic with regular oral analgesia remains the standard.

Deep peroneal (common peroneal): first web space; between EHL and EDL, beside the dorsalis pedis/anterior tibial artery.
Superficial peroneal (common peroneal): most of the dorsum except the first web space; subcutaneous ring from the tibial crest to the lateral malleolus.
Sural (tibial and common peroneal): lateral border of the foot and the fifth toe; subcutaneous between the lateral malleolus and the Achilles tendon.
Saphenous (femoral): medial ankle and foot; subcutaneous in front of the medial malleolus, around the great saphenous vein.
Advantages: no leg motor block, day case, low dose, avoids GA. Disadvantages: several injections, painful, no calf/thigh tourniquet cover, vein puncture.

Tibial onset is the slowest: wait and retest before repeating.
Top up the missed nerve under ultrasound within the dose limit, or ask for surgical infiltration, or convert to general anaesthesia.

Saphenous nerve block at and below the knee

The saphenous nerve is the only femoral branch below the knee: purely sensory, it supplies the medial leg, medial malleolus and inner foot. It completes a popliteal block. Position

Supine, the leg slightly externally rotated and the knee a little flexed over a pillow, so the medial side of the leg faces you. Stand on that side, screen beyond the foot.

Equipment
Linear probe; a tourniquet or elastic band for the thigh to fill the vein
50 mm echogenic needle (ultrasound) or a 23G hypodermic, as long as possible (landmark)
5 ml of 0.5% ropivacaine (ultrasound) or 5–10 ml (landmark)
Where to block it

The nerve leaves the adductor canal in the distal thigh, runs down between sartorius and gracilis to the medial knee, gives off the infrapatellar branch (skin below and inside the kneecap), then pierces the fascia and runs down the medial leg with the great saphenous vein to the front of the medial malleolus.

Below the knee, beside the vein (ultrasound paravenous): the viewer above. Superficial, no muscle, no artery: simple and quadriceps-sparing.
Below the knee, landmark field block: a subcutaneous ribbon from the tibial tuberosity to medial gastrocnemius (see Landmark field block).
Distal thigh, at the end of the adductor canal (distal subsartorial, or transsartorial): more reliable for the foot, still quadriceps-sparing when done low enough. See At the knee and above.
Adductor canal or femoral triangle: on the knee page; reliable but higher blocks can weaken vastus medialis.
Needle approach

Ultrasound: in-plane, shallow, in the fat; either direction. The tip stops next to the vein, on the nerve’s side, not in the vein. Keep probe pressure light or the vein (your landmark) disappears.

Sonoanatomy

Fat, the great saphenous vein (the black circle that collapses with pressure), the saphenous nerve as a small bright dot beside it (often not seen), the deep fascia, medial gastrocnemius behind and the bright medial surface of the tibia in front.

Target and deposition

Fluid surrounding the vein in the subcutaneous fat: the nerve, seen or not, lies within that ring. Fluid deep to the fascia (in gastrocnemius) or inside the vein is wrong.

Dose

USUAL VOLUME AND CONCENTRATION

5 ml of 0.5% ropivacaine (25 mg)

Ultrasound, beside the vein. Landmark field block: 5–10 ml of the same (25–50 mg). With a popliteal block (60 mg) the total is 85–110 mg: count it, and any surgical infiltration, against the patient’s maximum (about 3 mg/kg of ropivacaine, 210 mg at 70 kg). 0.5% matches the long popliteal block it usually accompanies; for the saphenous nerve on its own, 0.375% works as well.

Local anaesthetic toxicity: Keep the total dose within the maximum for the patient’s weight, especially with bilateral blocks or when combining blocks.

MECHANISM

Below the knee the saphenous nerve and its branches lie in the subcutaneous fat close to the great saphenous vein, superficial to the deep fascia. Fluid around the vein reaches them. The infrapatellar branch has already left above the injection, so the skin of the knee is not covered.

HOW DENSE, HOW RELIABLE

Even without ultrasound, injecting beside the visible vein blocked the nerve in all 20 volunteers in its first description, against about a third with blind subcutaneous infiltration; with ultrasound the success is high (around 90% in a trial of the infracondylar approach). The landmark field block is among the least reliable approaches, especially for the medial foot. The territory of the saphenous nerve on the foot varies: the medial dorsal branch of the superficial peroneal nerve may supply part of it.

WHAT IT MISSES
The knee (infrapatellar branch, femoral and obturator branches).
Everything else below the knee: it is a companion to a popliteal or ankle block, not a block on its own for most surgery.
Complications and how to avoid them
Bruising and haematoma: the vein is right there; aspirate, light pressure, and press afterwards.
Intravascular injection into the vein: aspirate before each aliquot.
Nerve injury: rare; the nerve is small and superficial.
Failure: commonest with the landmark technique; check before the incision.
Practical pearls
The saphenous is the only femoral nerve below the knee: medial leg, medial malleolus, inner foot.
Find the vein, find the nerve. Light pressure, or the vein vanishes.
A thigh band fills the vein and makes the target obvious.
Ring the vein, not the inside of it: aspirate.
Below-knee blocks spare the knee skin and the quadriceps.
For foot surgery, a low adductor canal block is the most reliable saphenous block.
Landmark field block: subcutaneous, not intradermal; inject as you withdraw.
Landmark field block (below the knee)

The classic technique, needing nothing but a needle. From the tibial tuberosity, lay 5–10 ml subcutaneously round the medial leg, posteriorly to the anterior border of medial gastrocnemius. Advance the needle fully, then inject while withdrawing. Not intradermal; a long strip may need two or three entry points. It hurts more than the ultrasound block, and it fails more often: use it when there is no probe, and test before the incision.

At the knee and above: the distal adductor canal
Distal subsartorial (end of the adductor canal): probe transverse on the medial thigh in the distal third, roughly a hand’s breadth above the patella, where the femoral artery leaves the canal through the adductor hiatus to become the popliteal artery. The target is just distal to where the saphenous nerve crosses the adductor magnus tendon, under sartorius, beside the saphenous branch of the descending genicular artery. 5–10 ml there blocked the saphenous nerve reliably with ambulation intact in a recent case series, and staining reached a nerve to vastus medialis only occasionally in cadavers.
Transsartorial: just above the medial femoral condyle, through sartorius to the fat beneath it (ultrasound, or by loss of resistance). In volunteers the transsartorial approach was more reliable for the medial foot than the field block or a block at the medial condyle.
Infracondylar: just below the medial tibial condyle, the nerve between the aponeuroses of sartorius and gracilis: as reliable as the subsartorial approach in a randomised trial.
Higher still (mid-thigh adductor canal, femoral triangle): reliable, but the higher you go the more likely the vastus medialis and quadriceps are weakened. See the knee page.
Consultant corner
Which saphenous block for which job. Forefoot: often not needed. Medial ankle, ankle fixation, medial malleolus: a distal adductor canal or below-knee paravenous block. Below-knee amputation: the saphenous at the adductor canal (or the femoral nerve) to cover the anteromedial skin and the tibial periosteum.
Quadriceps sparing matters most in day-case and frail patients who will be on crutches with a popliteal foot drop on the same leg: a weak knee as well makes falls likely.
Varicose veins, obesity, oedema make the paravenous view harder; go up to the distal adductor canal, where the artery is the landmark.
The medial foot gap: if the inner border of the foot is still sensate after a good saphenous block, it may be the medial branch of the superficial peroneal nerve: a small subcutaneous wheal over the dorsum of the first metatarsal fixes it.
Calf cuff: the saphenous covers the medial skin under the cuff; the sciatic covers the muscle. Together they make the cuff tolerable.
Frontier: what’s new
Distal subsartorial compartment block: a recently described target just distal to the adductor hiatus, aimed at blocking the saphenous nerve alone for foot and ankle surgery while sparing the quadriceps.
Distal adductor canal or below the knee? For foot and ankle surgery both spare the quadriceps when the injection is distal to the nerve to vastus medialis. The distal canal block uses the artery as its landmark and covers the medial foot more reliably; the below-knee paravenous block avoids the thigh altogether but depends on finding the vein. Choose by body habitus, the veins, and whether the patient is lateral or supine for the popliteal block.
Selective infrapatellar branch blocks are being mapped with ultrasound for knee arthroscopy and to treat painful infrapatellar neuromas after knee surgery.
Exam corner

PRACTICE QUESTION

A patient has had a popliteal sciatic block for an ankle fracture fixation. The medial malleolus and the medial side of the incision are still sensate. Explain why, and describe two ways to block the nerve responsible.

Model answer points
The saphenous nerve (terminal sensory branch of the femoral nerve, L3–L4) supplies the medial leg, the medial malleolus and the inner foot; it is not part of the sciatic nerve.
Ultrasound paravenous block below the knee: transverse at the tibial tuberosity, thigh band to fill the great saphenous vein, in-plane, 5 ml around the vein.
Distal adductor canal (subsartorial) block: 5–10 ml under sartorius near the adductor hiatus; reliable for the foot, quadriceps largely spared.
Landmark field block: 5–10 ml subcutaneously from the tibial tuberosity to medial gastrocnemius, injecting while withdrawing; less reliable.
Check the total local anaesthetic dose with the popliteal block.

PRACTICE QUESTION

Compare the approaches to the saphenous nerve for foot and ankle surgery.

Model answer points
Femoral triangle / mid-thigh adductor canal: reliable, may weaken vastus medialis and the quadriceps.
Distal adductor canal / subsartorial / transsartorial: reliable for the foot, quadriceps spared when done low.
Below the knee, paravenous with ultrasound: simple, superficial, high success; harder with varicose veins or obesity; vein puncture.
Below-knee landmark field block: no equipment, but the least reliable and more painful.
At the ankle: in front of the medial malleolus around the great saphenous vein; covers only the medial ankle and foot.

Forefoot: bunion, toe and ray surgery

BLOCK
Ankle block (all five nerves) for an ankle cuff; or popliteal + saphenous for a calf cuff or longer analgesia.
WHY
The incision and the osteotomy are all below the ankle. Deep peroneal and tibial supply the bone. The saphenous territory usually ends at the medial midfoot, short of the first tarsometatarsal joint, so for a bunion it can usually be left out; the dorsomedial skin of the first metatarsal is mainly superficial peroneal (medial dorsal cutaneous branch). Add the saphenous if the incision runs back towards the midfoot.

Day case: the ankle block lets the patient walk on the heel sooner. No adrenaline in a digital or web-space block.

The usual pairs

Count the milligrams when adding a saphenous block to a popliteal block (60 + 25 = 85 mg of ropivacaine), and more again if the surgeon infiltrates. A common teaching maximum for ropivacaine is about 3 mg/kg (about 210 mg at 70 kg), lower in frail older patients; use lean body weight.

STEP 1 OF 4 · SCAN

Probe transverse at the popliteal crease. Colour Doppler: find the popliteal artery (deepest), the vein just superficial to it, and the tibial nerve superficial to both. Then slide cephalad, following the tibial nerve, until the common peroneal nerve joins it from the lateral side. The junction is usually 5–10 cm above the crease, but find it in every patient.

STEP 2 OF 4 · IDENTIFY

Medial: semitendinosus over semimembranosus. Lateral: biceps femoris. Between them, in fat: the tibial (bigger, medial) and common peroneal (smaller, lateral) nerves inside one paraneural sheath. Lost them? Tilt the probe caudally (anisotropy) and ask the patient to point and pull up the foot: the nerves rock (the see-saw sign).

STEP 3 OF 4 · NEEDLE

In-plane, lateral to medial. Enter on the lateral thigh 2–3 cm from the probe, through or under biceps femoris, so the needle is nearly flat and bright. The sheath tents, then gives with a pop. Stop with the tip between the two nerves, inside the sheath.

Aspirate, then 1–2 ml: the fluid should part the two nerves and spread around them under the sheath, deep and superficial. Then the rest in 5 ml aliquots, aspirating between. Low pressure only; stop if it is stiff or the patient feels pain or a shock down the leg.

Probe transverse just above and behind the medial malleolus, marker towards the Achilles tendon. Colour Doppler: find the posterior tibial artery first. For heel surgery, slide 5–10 cm higher: you block the nerve before its calcaneal branches leave and the bone no longer breaks probe contact.

STEP 2 OF 4 · IDENTIFY

From front to back: Tibialis posterior, flexor Digitorum longus, Artery (with veins), Nerve, flexor Hallucis longus: “Tom, Dick, And Nervous Harry”. The nerve is a honeycomb just posterior to the artery. Tendon or nerve? Slide up: tendons turn into muscle, the nerve stays a nerve. Flexing the big toe makes FHL slide under it.

STEP 3 OF 4 · NEEDLE

In-plane from posterior, at a shallow angle in front of the Achilles tendon. The tip gives through the flexor retinaculum and stops beside the nerve, away from the artery. Keep off the tibial periosteum.

STEP 4 OF 4 · INJECT

1 ml first to see the spread, then the rest of 5 ml, aspirating between. The fluid should ring the nerve and lift the retinaculum from below. Block the tibial nerve first: it has the slowest onset.

STEP 1 OF 4 · SCAN

Probe transverse on the front of the ankle, at the extensor retinaculum (just above the joint line). Colour Doppler finds the anterior tibial artery lying on the tibia.

STEP 2 OF 4 · IDENTIFY

Ask the patient to lift the big toe: extensor hallucis longus moves. The deep peroneal nerve is a small dot beside the artery, usually lateral, sometimes medial (it crosses the artery near the ankle). Find the nerve on each scan; if you cannot, aim for fluid around the artery.

STEP 3 OF 4 · NEEDLE

In-plane from lateral, shallow, through the retinaculum and the edge of extensor digitorum longus. Stop beside the nerve, off the artery and off the tibial periosteum.

STEP 4 OF 4 · INJECT

1 ml, aspirate, then 2 ml: 3 ml in all. The fluid outlines the nerve and artery beneath the retinaculum. Injection under the periosteum hurts: withdraw a little if the patient winces.

STEP 1 OF 4 · SCAN

Leg slightly externally rotated. A tourniquet or elastic band on the thigh (not tight enough to stop arterial flow) fills the vein. Probe transverse on the medial leg at the level of the tibial tuberosity, with very light pressure.

STEP 2 OF 4 · IDENTIFY

The great saphenous vein is the round black circle in the fat, just behind the medial border of the tibia, over medial gastrocnemius. The saphenous nerve runs beside it (often posterior), superficial to the deep fascia: a small bright dot, or not seen at all.

STEP 3 OF 4 · NEEDLE

In-plane, from posterior here (either direction works), shallow, in the fat. The tip stops next to the vein, not in it, on the side where the nerve is.

STEP 4 OF 4 · INJECT

Aspirate, then 5 ml in small aliquots: the fluid should surround the vein (and the nerve with it). Release the thigh band afterwards. Expect a small bruise sometimes: the vein is close.

STEP 1 OF 4 · LANDMARKS

Supine, knee slightly flexed and the leg externally rotated. Find the tibial tuberosity and, behind the medial border of the tibia, the bulge of the medial head of gastrocnemius. If you can see or feel the great saphenous vein, mark it: the nerve runs with it.

STEP 2 OF 4 · IDENTIFY

The saphenous nerve and its branches lie in the subcutaneous fat between the tibia and gastrocnemius, close to the vein. A ribbon of local anaesthetic laid across that strip catches them, wherever they are.

STEP 3 OF 4 · NEEDLE

An ordinary hypodermic needle (23G, as long as you have). Enter at the tibial tuberosity and advance subcutaneously (not intradermally, not into muscle) towards the medial gastrocnemius, all the way. Aspirate: the vein is on the path.

STEP 4 OF 4 · INJECT

Inject while withdrawing, laying a continuous ribbon of 5–10 ml under the skin. A long gap may need a second entry point. It stings more than the ultrasound block, and it fails more often: check the medial leg after 15–20 minutes.
